q: Before rubber golf balls, what was packed tightly inside an early leather-covered golf ball?
d: Wet leather and feathers were packed together; drying produced a compact, hard ball.
evidence: Guide describes featheries made from leather and goose feathers.

q: The nineteenth-century guttie transformed golf using a material obtained from what?
d: Gutta-percha could be molded into a ball, replacing laboriously stuffed leather designs.
evidence: Guide identifies gutta-percha as tree sap and describes its use in balls.

q: Why can a dimpled golf ball travel farther than an otherwise similar smooth one?
d: The dimples change the thin layer of air around the ball, helping it stay attached longer and reducing the wake.
choices: Its dimples make the rubber springier
Its dimples increase the ball’s mass
evidence: Guide links dimples, turbulent boundary layer and reduced drag.

q: Before new tennis balls leave the factory, what treatment can fluff up their felt covers?
d: A gentle steaming raises the cover’s fibers before the balls are packed.
evidence: Bouncing Along explicitly describes gentle steaming to fluff the cover.

q: Babolat says its modern natural-gut tennis strings are made from the intestines of which animals?
d: The company switched from sheep gut to cow gut in the 1960s. The finished strings retain the name natural gut.
evidence: Manufacturer’s Myths and Facts section specifies bovine intestines since the 1960s.

q: Joseph Friedman formed the ridges in his prototype bendable drinking straw using a screw and what bathroom item?
d: He wound floss around the paper and into the screw’s threads, making corrugations that could bend.
evidence: Archive-based account describes a screw inside the straw and floss wound around it.

q: Before rubber became popular in the early twentieth century, bowling balls were commonly made from what?
d: The International Bowling Museum’s historical guide places the change from wood to rubber around 1905.
evidence: Exhibit guide explicitly states wood balls gave way to rubber in 1905.

q: Why do competitive squash players hit their ball repeatedly before play begins?
a: Warming it makes it bounce more
d: A double-yellow-dot squash ball has little bounce when cold. Repeated impacts bring it toward playing temperature.
choices: The impacts reduce its internal pressure
The impacts polish its surface for better grip
Cooling it makes it rebound faster
Warming it makes it bounce more
evidence: Federation describes initially low bounce and warming through several minutes of hitting.

q: What landing problem helped prompt the 1986 redesign of the men’s javelin?
d: Moving its center of gravity forward encouraged the point to descend, making valid landings easier to judge.
choices: Tips sticking too deeply to retrieve
Javelins rolling out of the sector
evidence: World Athletics explains four-centimeter forward center-of-gravity change and fewer flat landings.

q: What kitchen appliance did Bill Bowerman use while experimenting with a gripping sole for Nike running shoes?
d: The cooking grid suggested a pattern of projecting studs that could grip a running surface.
evidence: Nike archive documents waffle-iron experiments with shoe-sole material.

q: Where was Bill Bowerman’s original experimental shoe-making waffle iron rediscovered decades later?
d: His family found the discarded iron while working on the property. It had become an artifact of Nike’s early experiments.
evidence: Nike archive recounts rediscovery in a rubbish pit on the family property.

q: Which institution bought the first commercial batch of Joseph Friedman’s flexible straws?
d: Patients could position the bendable straw while lying down. The disposable design also avoided fragile glass drinking tubes.
evidence: Archive account identifies a hospital as the first sale in 1947 and explains patient use.

q: The 1953 Zamboni Model C11 ice resurfacer was built around what familiar vehicle?
d: The machine used a Willys CJ-3B as its body and went to the University of Denver.
evidence: Restoration account explicitly identifies a Willys Jeep CJ-3B base.

q: The first Wiffle Ball experiments used hollow plastic spheres originally intended to package what?
d: David Mullany cut different openings into packaging spheres until a design could curve easily through the air.
evidence: Company history identifies spheres from a nearby Coty cosmetics plant.

q: The name Wiffle came from neighborhood slang for what baseball event?
d: A strikeout was a whiff; the inventors dropped the h to name their lightweight ball.
evidence: Company history explicitly gives whiff as the source of WIFFLE.

q: A 2011 laboratory study tested corked baseball bats. What supposed advantage did it find no evidence for?
d: Removing wood changed the bat’s weight, but inserting cork did not give the collision the claimed springboard effect.
s: American Journal of Physics / University of Illinois
evidence: Paper reports no trampoline effect and discusses reduced inertia and faster swings separately.

q: According to Lamar Hunt’s account, which children’s toy helped inspire the name Super Bowl?
d: His children’s high-bouncing toy supplied the sound of the name he initially offered as a joke.
evidence: Official biography attributes Super Bowl to his children’s Super Ball toy.

q: Before children modeled with it, the product that became Play-Doh was sold to do what household job?
d: The soft compound lifted dirt from wallpaper before it found a much larger market as a modeling toy.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
evidence: Museum history traces the product to Kutol wallpaper cleaner.

q: What change in home heating helped undermine demand for the wallpaper cleaner that became Play-Doh?
a: Switch from coal to oil or gas heating
d: Oil and gas heating left less soot on walls, shrinking the cleaner’s original market before its reinvention as a toy.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
choices: Switch from coal to oil or gas heating
A move from radiators to fireplaces
Widespread use of indoor wood stoves
evidence: Museum explicitly links postwar oil/gas conversions to less soot and falling cleaner sales.

q: Sherman Poppen made the first Snurfer, an ancestor of the snowboard, by fastening together what?
d: He joined the skis and added a rope at the front for his daughters to hold.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
evidence: Museum’s prototype description and history document the paired skis.

q: Brunswick’s early manufactured Snurfer boards used laminated wood also used for which bowling-alley feature?
d: The company adapted an existing wood product to make the predecessor of modern snowboards.
s: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
evidence: Museum history explicitly identifies laminated wood used for bowling alley gutters.

q: The foam that became the Nerf ball first appeared in a proposed game inspired by which television family?
d: The game involved throwing soft foam rocks. Parker Brothers kept the foam-ball idea and dropped the larger game.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
evidence: Museum describes Flintstones inspiration and foam rocks in the abandoned game.

q: According to The Strong museum, the name Nerf borrowed slang associated with padding on what?
d: The soft indoor ball took its name from protective vehicle padding.
s: The Strong National Museum of Play
evidence: Museum explicitly identifies slang for off-road roll-bar padding.

q: A Winmau bristle dartboard is packed with which fiber, rather than animal bristles?
d: The densely packed fibers allow darts to enter and help the surface close up when they are removed.
evidence: Manufacturer specifies sisal fibers and self-healing behavior.

q: What safety concern helped drive international table tennis away from celluloid balls?
d: The federation sought alternatives that were easier to store and transport without celluloid’s fire risk.
evidence: ITTF retrospective identifies flammability as a driver of its material transition.

q: A device counting what on a steamship helped inspire James Ritty’s mechanical cash register?
d: Ritty saw a way to adapt mechanical counting to record transactions at his saloon.
evidence: Biography explicitly links propeller-revolution counter to register inspiration.

q: The Ritty brothers’ successful early cash register lacked which feature that now seems fundamental?
d: It recorded amounts entered with keys, but storage for the money came later.
evidence: Biography explicitly states the successful third prototype had no cash drawer.

q: OXO’s first Good Grips kitchen tool grew out of a struggle with arthritis while using what?
d: Sam and Betsey Farber developed an easier-to-hold handle after an ordinary metal peeler hurt her hands.
evidence: Brand history describes Betsey’s arthritis and the original peeler.

q: What industrial installation helped inspire James Dyson’s bagless vacuum technology?
d: He adapted cyclonic separation first to collect paint powder and then to remove household dust.
evidence: Biography identifies a timber-mill cyclone and its factory and vacuum applications.

q: James Dyson’s early household test of a bagless vacuum used a homemade cyclone built from what?
d: He strapped the experimental separator to an existing upright cleaner in place of its bag.
evidence: Biography specifies rudimentary cardboard cyclone strapped to an upright.

q: What unusual motion distinguished Dyson’s short-lived washing machine introduced in 2000?
a: Two drums turning in opposite directions
d: Its paired counter-rotating drums were an ambitious alternative to the usual single rotating drum.
choices: Laundry floating in a stationary tank
Two drums turning in opposite directions
A drum traveling up and down rails
evidence: Biography describes two large counter-rotating drums and commercial discontinuation.

q: Why did Britain’s Royal Air Force take an early interest in Bíró’s ballpoint pen?
a: It worked well at high altitude
d: The pen’s ink delivery avoided the pressure-related difficulties of fountain pens in aircraft.
choices: Its ink vanished after a day
It worked well at high altitude
Its tip could write through gloves
evidence: Biography links British adoption to reliable high-altitude ink delivery.

q: What household appliance helped Forrest Parry attach magnetic tape to a plastic card during its development?
d: His wife suggested heat-bonding the stripe while she was ironing. The experiment worked.
evidence: IBM account credits his wife’s ironing suggestion with bonding the stripe.

q: Before credit cards adopted magnetic stripes, Parry’s early striped-card project was intended for what?
d: The original aim was secure identification; banking and transport became major later uses.
evidence: IBM history explicitly states more secure identity cards for CIA officials.

q: Why did early floppy disks acquire protective sleeves with a special inner lining?
d: The flexible magnetic disks got dirty easily. A wiping element inside the envelope made handling them more practical.
choices: To prevent the disk from spinning
evidence: IBM describes slim envelopes equipped with an innovative dust-wiping element.

q: An early Canadian military trackball used a ball borrowed from which sport?
d: The ball helped operators select targets in a computerized naval defense system.
evidence: DATAR caption explicitly identifies Canadian five-pin bowling ball.

q: On Engelbart’s early computer mouse, where did the cable emerge relative to the user’s hand?
d: The wire originally trailed toward the user, rather than forward beyond the fingertips.
choices: From the top under the palm
evidence: Museum states the wire tail originally came out under the user’s wrist.

q: What everyday railway practice inspired Herman Hollerith’s use of punched cards to record personal data?
d: Patterns of holes could represent traveler details. Hollerith applied machine-readable holes to census records.
evidence: IBM names conductors’ position-coded ticket holes as inspiration.

q: NCR’s unusual CRAM computer storage system selected a magnetic card by doing what physically?
d: The cards hung in a deck until the mechanism released the selected one for processing.
choices: Pulling it through a vacuum tube
evidence: Timeline describes Mylar cards suspended on rods and dropped individually.

q: Unlike modern plastic recording tape, UNIVAC’s early UNISERVO computer tape was made from what?
d: A coated phosphor-bronze strip carried the data. A full reel could weigh about three pounds.
evidence: Timeline specifies phosphor-bronze tape with metallic coating and three-pound reels.

q: What kept the read head in IBM’s pioneering RAMAC disk system from scraping the spinning disks?
d: The head had to hover above the magnetic surface; touching it could destroy stored data.
evidence: IBM describes compressed air used to keep the head hovering.

q: What unpleasant factory job did the early Unimate robot take over at General Motors?
d: The heavy robotic arm moved die-cast parts according to instructions stored on a magnetic drum.
evidence: Timeline identifies sequencing and stacking hot die-cast pieces in 1961.

q: Instead of touching down on wheels, how did the experimental Ryan X-13 Vertijet finish its vertical landing?
d: A raised platform on a trailer caught the aircraft; the platform could then be lowered horizontally.
s: National Museum of the US Air Force
evidence: Museum photo caption describes cable at top of raised trailer platform.

q: What rescue scheme was proposed for Goodyear’s inflatable airplane?
a: Drop it to a stranded pilot to inflate and fly out
d: The compact aircraft could be delivered near a downed pilot behind enemy lines. The project never became a standard rescue system.
s: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum
choices: Inflate it around a sinking ship
Drop it to a stranded pilot to inflate and fly out
Fly it as an unmanned rescue balloon
evidence: Museum long description explicitly states behind-enemy-lines drop, inflation and escape concept.

q: The museum-preserved Imperial factory shunter had no firebox. What energy supply was replenished between its journeys?
d: Its pressure reservoir was replenished from factory steam mains, then supplied the cylinders during short trips.
choices: Hot oil supplied from a furnace
evidence: Collection description explains pressure vessel charged from factory mains.

q: What unusual wheel equipment did Michelin put on its Micheline railcars to soften the ride?
d: Special tires and guide rings allowed the vehicles to run on narrow railway tracks.
evidence: Company history describes railcars on special guided tires.

q: In a 2025 brewing study, which molecule in yeast extracts made lager cloudy by interacting with its proteins?
d: The extracts offered researchers another way to create haze, a prized feature of some beer styles.
evidence: ACS study summary attributes haze to yeast-extract RNA and beer proteins.

q: Ford and McDonald’s collaborated on car-part composites using which byproduct of coffee roasting?
d: Coffee chaff was heated and mixed with plastic and additives for components such as headlamp housings.
evidence: 2019 announcement describes dried bean skins, low-oxygen heating and headlamp-housing composite.

q: BMW’s color-changing iX Flow concept borrowed display technology familiar from which device?
d: Electrical signals moved charged light and dark pigments in a special body film, changing the car’s appearance.
evidence: 2022 release explicitly compares electrically driven pigment capsules to e-readers.

q: What creates the tiny stars in a Rolls-Royce Starlight Headliner?
d: Craftspeople place fibers at different angles and depths to vary the light, and can reproduce a personally chosen star pattern.
choices: Holes illuminated by a ceiling projector
evidence: Manufacturer describes individually inserted fibers in hand-placed perforations.
